what_its_for: Sorafenib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of kidney cancer, liver cancer, and thyroid cancer. It works by slowing down or stopping the growth of cancer cells and blocking the blood supply that tumors need to grow.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablets whole with a full glass of water. Take sorafenib on an empty stomach — either 1 hour before a meal or 2 hours after a meal. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets. Try to take it at the same times every day to help you remember.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 400 mg (two 200 mg tablets) taken twice a day, approximately 12 hours apart. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how well you tolerate the medicine and how your cancer responds. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribed — do not take more or less.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next scheduled dose at the regular time. Do not take a double dose to make up for the one you missed. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store sorafenib tablets at room temperature between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed and store it in a dry place away from heat, moisture, and light. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not store in the bathroom.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking sorafenib with food, especially high-fat meals, as this can reduce how well the medicine works. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as they may affect how the drug works in your body. Do not take herbal supplements such as St. John's Wort without first talking to your doctor. Avoid aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, or other blood-thinning medicines unless your doctor says it is safe. Protect your hands and feet from friction, heat, and pressure, as sorafenib can cause a painful skin reaction. Use sunscreen and protective clothing when going outdoors, as this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to the sun.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: chest pain or pressure; sudden severe headache, confusion, or trouble speaking or walking (signs of stroke or bleeding in the brain); coughing or vomiting blood; unusual bruising or bleeding; severe blistering or peeling of your skin; extreme pain, redness, swelling, or sores on your hands or feet (hand-foot skin reaction); high blood pressure that is hard to control; shortness of breath or swelling in your legs; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; signs of a hole in your stomach or intestines such as sudden severe abdominal pain. Also call your doctor if you develop any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Sorafenib may start working soon after you begin treatment, but it may take several weeks or months before your doctor can confirm the medicine is working through scans or blood tests. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor, even if you feel okay, because cancer treatment often continues even when you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and over): Generally safe to use, but older patients may be more sensitive to side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to monitor you more closely or adjust your dose if you have moderate or severe liver disease. Sorafenib is not recommended in severe liver impairment. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Sorafenib can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Men with partners who could become pregnant should use a condom during treatment and for 3 months after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking sorafenib and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Children: Sorafenib is not approved for use in children and adolescents under 18 years of age.
